blogs.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
blogs.description: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. blogs.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
blogs.description: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" blogs.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
blogs.description: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

blogs.title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
blogs.description: Perplexity crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate today , CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor at a live event. The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B , with Cursor crossing $4.6B ), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025 , and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard . AI Twitter Recap Qwen4-Max in the wild Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals : Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions ( Arena ). WebDev : It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor ( WebDev ). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol ( I2WebDev ). Vals Index : It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance ( Vals ). Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). Vision results (independent) : Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 ( Transluce ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models ( balesni ). Goodfire acquisition talks : The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs ( report ). Other integrity signals : Benchmark contamination : Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval ( Karvonen ). Incident taxonomy : OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents ( framework ). Disclosure policy : Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities ( policy ). Inference systems and agent infrastructure Together moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeup DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Vera Rubin : vLLM with Dynamo on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark shows 63.4x per-chip throughput over GB300 NVL72 at 400 tok/s/user, and 93.3x at 600 ( vLLM ). Batch-1 latency : SGLang-adjacent work reaches ~2,500 tok/s at batch size 1 on TP4, 1.7x its GB300 result ( saltyph ). Baseten reports a similar 1.7x over its 4xB300 numbers ( Baseten ). Agent-driven optimization : An agent shared Engram tables across HBM via NVLink symmetric memory to recover prefix-cache capacity ( Liu ). Another team says agents found optimizations that made its B300 step time 10% faster ( Halex ). Agentic serving research : MIT's Evolving Infra replaces fixed prefill/decode disaggregation with online adaptation. Against NVIDIA Dynamo on up to 256 GB300s, it reports up to 4.1x lower latency and 14x lower P95 TTFT ( Evolving Infra ). Pipeline-parallel prefill : Inferact finds PP2 on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash sustains 23% more requests per GPU than DEP2 at a 2s TTFT target ( Inferact ). Prefix-cache pitfalls : Ollama found that a single system-prompt timestamp or a change in reasoning effort can wipe the cache ( Ollama ). Sandboxes and training : External sandboxes : Simon Willison describes running agents on a Mac while executing their code in WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandboxes. The pattern includes allow-list proxies and credential replacement ( post ). MLPerf : In MLPerf Training v6.1, a GB300 NVL72 trained GPT-OSS-20B in 19.7 minutes, 2.86x faster than H100 ( Lambda ). One endpoint for open models. Hugging Face Inference Providers now runs on OpenRouter using the same endpoint and token. Hugging Face Research, benchmarks and evals PyBot : A swarm of 1,000 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agents spent a week writing a rule-based chatbot with no neural network ( lewtun ). Scale : The agents exchanged ~175k messages and merged ~8k PRs. Result : The bot is 630k lines of Python with zero dependencies and is reported on par with SmolLM-360M on everyday questions. Self-improvement and training : AutoRL : Agents supervising a live RL run lifted Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% ( omarsar0 ). Benchmark-gaming caveat : A roundup warns that many self-improving agent gains come from learning the benchmark rather than the task ( TuringPost ). Weight-space programming : Opus 5.5 hand-wrote transformer weights that solved algorithmic tasks with a median of 166 parameters ( dair_ai ). Data curation : DatologyAI published the tech report behind its claimed 6x pretraining compute multiplier ( Datology ). Distillation reproduction : A small-scale replication confirms perturbed-input distillation helps when the student trains from scratch, but finds it hurts when distilling into a pretrained student ( Maini ). New benchmarks : GradeBench : The best frontier model agrees with instructors only 57% of the time when grading handwritten physics answers ( GradeBench ). Time to First Audio : AA's new TTS latency benchmark finds a median of 376 ms for streaming models versus 2.0 s for non-streaming ones ( AA ). SpeedRunBench : Inkling-2-Small cleared SuperTux 1-1 in 1,988 frames, ahead of Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol ( SpeedRunBench ). Science models and developer tools Gemini 4 Carbon : DeepMind says Carbon powered AlphaProof Code agents that verified Signal's cryptographic code. It also spotted wet-lab errors and found 40x more related protein sequences ( details ). Science access : Google expanded free Carbon access for 10,000 scientists through Antigravity ( program ). Context window : Antigravity doubled the context window for Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, cutting compaction 3.5x per user turn ( Mohan ). User reports (anecdotal) : One researcher says Carbon solved a problem that waves of Astra and Fable attempts had not ( anecdote ). OpenAI for science and health : OpenAI is opening free frontier access to up to 200,000 scientists, with applications from Nov 23 ( program ). Productivity study : OpenAI reports scientists roughly doubled their productivity in a study of 1,800 participants ( study ). Physics showcase : Physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model ( blog ). Healthcare : ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and more than 20 plugins ( healthcare ). Claude Code : The desktop app now runs iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator and can fold and unfold the device to test layouts ( ClaudeDevs ). Verification : The team published how it uses cheap tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs to let Claude verify its own work ( blog ). Unreleased model (unconfirmed) : A "Silicon 2" entry spotted in Devin is suspected to be an Anthropic model ( rumor ). Liquid d1.2-ultra : It ranks #1 on AA's Decision Index at $0.042 per M input tokens ( AA ). Sage S2.1 Flash : The open-weight science model reports leading MLE-bench Lite and OfficeQA Pro results ( Sage ). FLUX-mimic-x : A 7B video-action robotics model ranks #1 on RoboLab among real-time models ( mimic ). Unsloth computer use : Local models can now drive desktop apps and game engines through Unsloth ( Unsloth ). Industry and policy Nvidia. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ).
